chunks: Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ibn Muskān from Sulaymān ibn Khālid who said:

I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) about what will be faced by one who is [buried] in the grave, so he said, ‘Verily two angels who are called Munkar and Nakīr will come to the one who is in the grave and will ask him about the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) saying, “What do you have to say about this man who rose among you?” He will ask, “Who was he?” They will say, “The one who used to say that he is the Messenger of Allah. Was that true?” So if the man was one of the doubters, he will say, “I do not know. I heard the people saying [that] but I do not know whether it was the truth or a lie.” So they will strike him such a blow that it will be audible to the inhabitants of the heavens and the inhabitants of earth, except the polytheists. But if he was one of those with certitude, he will not fear and will say [confidently], “Are you asking me about the Messenger of Allah?” So they will ask, “Do you know that he is the Messenger of Allah?” He will say, “I bear witness that he is the Messenger of Allah in truth. He came with guidance and the religion of truth.” Thus he will see his position in Paradise and his grave will be expanded for him. They (the two angels) will then say to him, “Sleep a slumber wherein there is no dream, in the best state of any sleeper.”’

key_terms.الشَّكِّ: Doubt (referring to the state of the deceased)
key_terms.الْبَرْزَخُ: The intermediate realm (implied by the context of the grave state)
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الْقَبْرِ: The inhabitant of the grave (the deceased)
key_terms.مَنْكَرٌ وَنَكِيرٌ: Munkar and Nakīr (the two angels who question the dead)
key_terms.مُتَيَقِّنًا: One with certitude (referring to the state of the deceased)

ai.seo_question: What happens to the deceased in the grave during the questioning by Munkar and Nakīr?
ai.summary: This narration from *Kitab al-Zuhd* details the post-mortem interrogation by angels Munkar and Nakīr, emphasizing the pivotal role of certainty (*yaqīn*) versus doubt (*shakk*) regarding the Prophet’s prophethood. The text highlights the cosmic resonance of the doubter’s blow, audible to all heavens and earth, while the certitude-holder is granted a preview of Paradise and a dreamless, pleasant sleep in *Barzakh*. This underscores the Shia emphasis on inner conviction as the determinant of one’s state in the intermediate realm.
